passages.title: Hybrid Working Arrangements
passages.text: Since 2021, many professional services firms have moved to hybrid working models, in which employees split their week between the office and home. Supporters argue that hybrid arrangements improve staff retention, and a survey of 1,200 employees at mid-sized firms found that 64% would consider leaving their employer if required to return to the office full time. However, the evidence on productivity is less clear. Some studies report that individual output on focused tasks rises when employees work from home, while others find that collaboration and the informal transfer of knowledge suffer, particularly for junior staff who learn by observing colleagues. Managers also report difficulties in assessing performance when teams are rarely in the same place. As a result, a growing number of firms now specify 'anchor days' on which entire teams are expected to be present. Critics note that anchor days can lead to overcrowded offices on popular days and empty floors on others, which undermines the property savings that hybrid working was expected to deliver. Firms that have reduced their office space by more than a third have sometimes had to lease additional meeting rooms at short notice. The debate is therefore shifting away from whether hybrid working should continue, which most firms now accept, towards how it should be organised to balance flexibility, learning and cost.

passages.title: Supply Chain Finance
passages.text: Supply chain finance, sometimes called reverse factoring, allows a large buyer to arrange for its suppliers to be paid early by a bank. The supplier receives payment shortly after its invoice is approved, minus a small discount, and the bank is repaid by the buyer on the original due date, which may be 90 or even 120 days later. Because the discount is based on the buyer's credit rating rather than the supplier's, smaller suppliers can obtain cash more cheaply than they could through a conventional bank loan. For buyers, the arrangement makes it possible to extend payment terms without damaging relationships with suppliers. Accounting rules, however, have not always required buyers to disclose how much of their trade payables is financed in this way. Analysts have warned that this can make a company's debt appear lower than it effectively is, since the obligation to the bank behaves much like short-term borrowing. The risk became visible when several programmes were withdrawn at short notice: suppliers that had grown dependent on early payment faced sudden cash shortages, and buyers had to find funds to settle invoices on time. Recent changes to disclosure standards require companies to report the terms and size of such programmes, although they do not oblige companies to reclassify the amounts as debt.

passages.title: Recycling Electric Vehicle Batteries
passages.text: As sales of electric vehicles grow, attention is turning to what happens to their batteries at the end of their useful life. A typical vehicle battery retains around 70 to 80% of its original capacity when it is no longer suitable for driving, and such batteries can be reused for stationary energy storage, for example to balance supply from solar panels. Eventually, however, every battery must be recycled. Current recycling methods fall into two broad groups. Pyrometallurgical processes melt the battery down; they are well established and can handle many battery types, but they consume large amounts of energy and recover lithium poorly. Hydrometallurgical processes dissolve the materials in chemical solutions; they recover a higher share of lithium, cobalt and nickel but require batteries to be carefully sorted and pre-treated. The economics of recycling depend heavily on metal prices, and cobalt has historically been the most valuable component. When cobalt prices fell sharply in recent years, several recyclers found their margins squeezed. Meanwhile, concerns about the ethical sourcing of cobalt have led many manufacturers to design batteries that use little or no cobalt, which further reduces the value that recyclers can extract. Policymakers in several regions have introduced minimum recycled-content requirements for new batteries, intended to guarantee demand for recovered materials regardless of market prices. Industry groups broadly support these targets but argue that the deadlines are too ambitious given the limited number of batteries currently reaching the end of their life.

passages.title: Loan and Bond Covenants
passages.text: Covenants are promises that a borrower makes to its lenders in a loan or bond agreement. Maintenance covenants require the borrower to meet financial tests, such as a maximum ratio of net debt to EBITDA, at regular intervals, usually every quarter. Incurrence covenants, by contrast, are tested only when the borrower takes a specific action, such as raising additional debt or paying a dividend. Traditional bank loans have typically included maintenance covenants, whereas high-yield bonds have usually relied on incurrence covenants alone. Over the past decade, a large share of leveraged loans has been issued in a 'covenant-lite' form, meaning that they lack maintenance covenants and therefore resemble bonds in this respect. Lenders accepted these terms during a period of strong demand for higher-yielding assets. Supporters argue that covenant-lite structures prevent lenders from forcing a company into default because of a temporary dip in earnings. Critics respond that, without early warning signals, lenders may only be able to intervene once a company's position has deteriorated severely, which tends to reduce the amount they recover. Data from the most recent downturn are not yet sufficient to determine which view is correct, partly because many borrowers were able to refinance before their debts fell due.

passages.title: Pricing Subscription Software
passages.text: Many software companies have replaced one-off licence sales with subscriptions, under which customers pay a monthly or annual fee for continued access. For the vendor, subscriptions produce more predictable revenue and a closer, ongoing relationship with customers. For customers, the upfront cost is lower, although the total paid over several years can exceed the price of a perpetual licence. A key decision for subscription businesses is how to structure their pricing tiers. A common approach offers three tiers, with the middle tier designed to be the most attractive; research on consumer choice suggests that buyers presented with three options disproportionately select the middle one. Vendors also increasingly use usage-based pricing, charging according to the volume of data processed or the number of transactions handled. This aligns cost with the value a customer receives, but it makes revenue harder to forecast, since usage can fall sharply when a customer's own business slows. Investors evaluating subscription companies pay close attention to net revenue retention, which compares the revenue generated this year by a group of existing customers with the revenue the same group generated a year earlier. A figure above 100% indicates that expansion within existing accounts more than offsets the revenue lost from customers who cancel or downgrade.

passages.title: Central Bank Independence
passages.text: In most advanced economies, monetary policy is set by a central bank that operates independently of the government. The case for independence rests on the observation that elected politicians may be tempted to keep interest rates low before an election, boosting growth in the short term at the cost of higher inflation later. By delegating rate decisions to an institution with a clear mandate, usually an inflation target of around 2%, governments aim to make their commitment to price stability more credible. Historical comparisons show that countries with more independent central banks have, on average, experienced lower inflation, although economists disagree about how much of this difference is caused by independence itself rather than by other features of those countries, such as a broad public aversion to inflation. Independence is never absolute. Governments typically appoint central bank governors, set their mandates in law and can, in principle, change those laws. In addition, since the financial crisis of 2008, central banks have bought large quantities of government bonds, which has blurred the line between monetary policy and the financing of public spending. Some commentators argue that this has exposed central banks to greater political pressure, while others maintain that the purchases were justified by the need to prevent deflation and do not compromise independence as long as they are reversed in time.

passages.title: Screening Graduate Applicants
passages.text: Large employers that recruit graduates often receive tens of thousands of applications for a few hundred places. To manage this volume, most now use online assessments as an early screening stage, before any interview takes place. These typically include numerical and verbal reasoning tests and, increasingly, situational judgement tests, which present candidates with realistic workplace scenarios and ask them to rate possible responses. Employers value these tools because they are cheap to administer at scale and because scores on well-designed reasoning tests have been shown to predict later job performance better than unstructured interviews do. However, the tests are not without critics. Candidates from some educational backgrounds may have had less exposure to timed multiple-choice formats, and practice is known to improve scores, which raises questions about whether the tests measure ability or familiarity. Some employers have responded by publishing free practice materials, so that all applicants can become familiar with the format before sitting the real test. Others have introduced 'blind' screening, in which recruiters reviewing applications cannot see the candidate's university or name. A small number of firms have removed reasoning tests altogether, replacing them with short work-sample tasks, although there is not yet enough evidence to say whether this produces better hires.

passages.title: The Foundry Model in Semiconductors
passages.text: For most of the industry's history, semiconductor companies designed and manufactured their own chips. Since the late 1980s, however, a growing share of production has moved to foundries: specialised manufacturers that produce chips designed by other companies. This allowed the rise of 'fabless' firms, which focus entirely on design and outsource all manufacturing. The model works because building a leading-edge fabrication plant now costs well over ten billion dollars, an investment that only a handful of companies can justify. By pooling demand from many customers, a foundry can keep its plants running near full capacity, which is essential given the high fixed costs. The concentration of advanced manufacturing in a small number of locations has, however, raised concerns about supply security. During a recent period of chip shortages, carmakers in particular struggled to obtain the components they needed, because foundries prioritised customers with larger and more profitable orders. Several governments have since offered subsidies to encourage the construction of new plants within their borders. Analysts caution that subsidies alone may not be enough: a plant also requires a deep pool of skilled engineers and a network of specialised suppliers, both of which take many years to develop. Some integrated manufacturers have also begun offering foundry services to outside customers, blurring the distinction between the two models.

passages.title: Earn-outs in Acquisitions
passages.text: When a buyer and a seller cannot agree on the value of a business, they sometimes bridge the gap with an earn-out. Under this arrangement, part of the purchase price is paid upfront, and further payments are made only if the business meets agreed targets after completion, typically over one to three years. Targets are most often based on revenue or EBITDA, although some deals use non-financial milestones, such as obtaining regulatory approval for a new product. Earn-outs are particularly common in the acquisition of young, fast-growing companies, whose future performance is hard to predict, and in sectors such as life sciences and technology. They can also help retain the founders, who usually stay on to run the business during the earn-out period. However, earn-outs frequently lead to disputes. Once the business is part of a larger group, the buyer controls decisions on pricing, investment and the allocation of shared costs, all of which can affect whether targets are reached. Sellers may suspect that the buyer is deliberately suppressing performance to avoid paying, while buyers may suspect that sellers are boosting short-term results at the expense of long-term value. To reduce this risk, agreements often specify in detail how the relevant figures will be calculated and which decisions require the seller's consent. Even so, a significant proportion of earn-outs end in negotiation or litigation.

passages.title: Four-Day Week Trials
passages.text: Several companies have experimented with a four-day working week, in which staff work around 32 hours for the same pay they previously received for a five-day week. In one widely reported trial involving 60 organisations, most participating firms reported that revenue remained broadly stable over the six-month period, and a majority chose to continue with the arrangement after the trial ended. Employees reported lower levels of stress and fewer sick days. Supporters argue that the results show that much of the traditional working week is spent on low-value activity, such as unnecessary meetings, which can be eliminated without loss of output. Sceptics point out that the organisations taking part volunteered to do so, and are therefore likely to be those best suited to the change, such as office-based firms with flexible workloads. They also note that the trial measured outcomes over a relatively short period, and that initial enthusiasm may fade. Sectors that require continuous cover, such as healthcare and retail, face a different challenge: reducing individual hours means hiring additional staff or rearranging shifts, which may raise costs. A number of firms in these sectors have instead adopted compressed schedules, in which employees work the same total hours over four longer days.

passages.title: The Problem with ESG Ratings
passages.text: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings are intended to help investors assess how well companies manage non-financial risks and opportunities. Unlike credit ratings, which estimate a single, well-defined outcome, namely the probability of default, ESG ratings combine dozens of indicators, and providers differ in which indicators they include and how they weight them. As a result, the correlation between the ratings that different providers assign to the same company is much lower than the correlation between credit ratings. A company can be rated a leader by one provider and a laggard by another. Much of the underlying data comes from companies' own disclosures, which means that larger firms, with more resources to devote to reporting, tend to receive higher scores. Critics argue that this rewards disclosure rather than actual performance. Supporters counter that the diversity of approaches is a strength, since investors have different priorities and can choose the provider that best reflects their own. Regulators in several jurisdictions have begun to require rating providers to explain their methodologies and to manage conflicts of interest, such as selling consulting services to the companies they rate. These rules do not, however, prescribe a single methodology, so the dispersion between ratings is expected to persist.

passages.title: Rethinking Just-in-Time
passages.text: For several decades, manufacturers sought to minimise inventory through just-in-time production, under which components arrive shortly before they are needed. Holding less stock reduces the cash tied up in working capital, lowers storage costs and exposes quality problems quickly, since there is no buffer to hide defective parts. The approach was widely credited with improving the efficiency of car and electronics production. Its weakness is vulnerability to disruption: when a single supplier cannot deliver, an entire production line may stop. Recent disruptions, including factory closures and shipping delays, have led many firms to reconsider the balance between efficiency and resilience. Some have increased their safety stocks of critical components, while others have added second suppliers in different regions, even where these charge higher prices. Surveys of supply chain managers suggest that most intend to keep higher inventories for the foreseeable future. Yet holding extra stock is not free. A company with annual sales of 1 billion euros that raises its inventory from 30 to 45 days of sales ties up roughly an additional 40 million euros in working capital, before considering the cost of storage and the risk that goods become obsolete. Analysts therefore expect firms to target extra inventory at a small number of hard-to-replace components rather than increasing stock across the board.

passages.title: Open Banking
passages.text: Open banking rules require banks to share customer account data with authorised third-party providers, but only when the customer gives explicit consent. The data is transferred through standardised application programming interfaces, or APIs, rather than through the older practice of 'screen scraping', in which customers handed over their online banking passwords so that an app could log in on their behalf. Supporters of open banking argue that it increases competition by allowing new entrants to offer services such as budgeting tools, faster loan decisions and cheaper payments without having to build a bank. Take-up was slow at first: in one market, fewer than one in ten adults had used an open banking service three years after the rules came into force. Usage has since grown more quickly, driven mainly by payments made directly from bank accounts, which avoid card fees for merchants. Banks have raised concerns that they bear the cost of building and maintaining the interfaces while receiving little in return. Consumer groups, for their part, worry that customers may not fully understand what they are agreeing to when they give consent. Policymakers in several countries are now considering extending the model beyond current accounts to savings, pensions and insurance, an approach often described as 'open finance'.

passages.title: Revenue Management in Aviation
passages.text: Airlines were among the first businesses to adopt revenue management, the practice of varying prices according to expected demand in order to maximise the revenue earned from a fixed and perishable capacity. A seat that is empty when a flight departs can never be sold, so airlines try to fill every seat while charging each passenger as close as possible to the maximum they are willing to pay. To do this, they divide the cabin into many fare classes with different prices and conditions. Cheaper fares usually require booking well in advance and carry restrictions on changes or refunds, which makes them unattractive to business travellers, who often book late and need flexibility. As the departure date approaches, the system closes the cheaper fare classes once a set number of seats has been sold in them. Airlines also deliberately sell more tickets than there are seats on many routes, because a predictable proportion of passengers do not turn up. When more passengers arrive than expected, the airline must offer compensation to those who are denied boarding, and the rules governing this compensation vary between jurisdictions. Similar techniques are now used by hotels, car rental firms and event organisers, although the term 'dynamic pricing' is more common outside aviation.

passages.title: How Bank Capital Rules Work
passages.text: Banks fund their lending partly with deposits and borrowing and partly with equity, the capital provided by shareholders. Because equity absorbs losses before depositors and creditors are affected, regulators require banks to hold a minimum amount of capital relative to their risk-weighted assets. Under this approach, each loan or investment is assigned a risk weight: a loan to a highly rated government may carry a weight of zero, while an unsecured loan to a small business may carry a weight of 100% or more. A bank holding 10 billion euros of assets with an average risk weight of 50% therefore has risk-weighted assets of 5 billion euros, and a minimum capital ratio of 8% would require it to hold 400 million euros of capital. After the financial crisis of 2008, minimum requirements were raised and additional buffers were introduced, so that most large banks now hold substantially more capital than before. Banks argue that higher capital requirements raise their cost of funding and therefore the price of loans, since equity is a more expensive source of funding than debt. Some economists dispute this, noting that a better-capitalised bank is less risky, so its shareholders and creditors should demand lower returns. Because risk weights can be calculated using banks' own internal models, regulators have also introduced a simple leverage ratio, which compares capital to total assets without any risk weighting.

passages.title: The Rise of Private Credit
passages.text: Private credit refers to loans made to companies by non-bank lenders, such as specialist investment funds, rather than by banks or through publicly traded bonds. The market has expanded rapidly over the past fifteen years, partly because stricter capital rules made some types of lending less attractive for banks. Private credit funds typically lend to mid-sized companies, many of which are owned by private equity firms. Borrowers value the speed and certainty of execution: a single lender or a small group of lenders can agree terms in weeks, whereas a syndicated loan or bond issue requires marketing to many investors and is exposed to changes in market conditions. In return, borrowers usually pay a higher interest rate than they would on comparable bank loans. For investors, such as pension funds and insurers, private credit offers higher yields and floating-rate income, which rose when central banks increased interest rates. However, the loans are not traded, so their reported values are based on models rather than market prices and may adjust only slowly when conditions worsen. Some regulators have expressed concern that the sector's rapid growth has not been tested by a severe recession. Industry participants respond that private credit funds are mostly financed by long-term investors rather than by deposits, so they are less exposed to sudden withdrawals than banks.

passages.title: What Loyalty Programmes Are For
passages.text: Loyalty programmes reward customers for repeat purchases, usually through points that can be exchanged for discounts, products or services. Their stated purpose is to increase customer retention, but research suggests that their effect varies widely. Many members of loyalty schemes would have bought from the same company anyway, which means that a large share of the rewards is given to customers whose behaviour does not change. The main value of modern programmes may lie less in the rewards than in the data they generate. By linking purchases to individual customers, retailers can tailor offers, plan stock and measure the impact of promotions more precisely. Some retailers also earn significant income by selling insights derived from this data to the brands whose products they stock. Programmes also create a financial liability: points that have been issued but not yet redeemed represent a future cost, and companies must estimate how many will eventually be used. Points that are never redeemed, known as breakage, reduce this cost, and some programmes have been criticised for setting expiry rules designed to increase breakage. Airlines operate some of the largest schemes; their frequent-flyer programmes sell points in bulk to credit card issuers, and in some cases the programme has been valued at more than the airline itself.

passages.title: Cloud Repatriation
passages.text: Over the past fifteen years, many companies have moved their computing workloads from their own data centres to public cloud providers. The cloud allows firms to pay only for the capacity they use, to scale up quickly when demand rises and to avoid large upfront investments in hardware. For start-ups and businesses with unpredictable demand, these advantages are usually decisive. However, a number of established companies have recently moved some workloads back to their own facilities, a trend known as cloud repatriation. Their reasoning is that, for large and stable workloads, renting capacity indefinitely can cost more than owning it. One software company reported that it expected to save around 7 million dollars over five years by moving its main applications out of the cloud, after its annual cloud bill had reached 3.2 million dollars. Critics of repatriation point out that such estimates often exclude the cost of the specialist staff needed to run data centres, as well as the opportunity cost of management attention. Cloud providers, for their part, have responded by offering discounts for long-term capacity commitments. Most industry surveys indicate that total spending on public cloud services continues to grow, which suggests that repatriation remains limited to specific workloads rather than representing a broad reversal of the trend.

passages.title: Delivering Merger Synergies
passages.text: Most acquisitions are justified by synergies: cost savings or additional revenue that the combined company can achieve but that the two businesses could not achieve separately. Cost synergies, such as closing duplicate offices or combining purchasing, are generally easier to estimate and to deliver than revenue synergies, which depend on customers' decisions to buy more. For this reason, many buyers are reluctant to pay for revenue synergies when setting the price they offer. Studies of completed deals suggest that a significant proportion of acquisitions fail to deliver the synergies announced at the time of the deal, although definitions of failure vary from study to study. Common explanations include integration plans that are drawn up too late, the departure of key staff and clashes between the cultures of the two organisations. Cultural differences are hard to measure before a deal, since buyers usually have limited access to the target's employees during due diligence. Some acquirers therefore set up a dedicated integration team before completion, with clear targets for the first hundred days. Others deliberately keep the acquired business separate for a period, particularly when its value depends on an entrepreneurial culture that could be damaged by the procedures of a larger organisation. Neither approach guarantees success, and the right choice depends on the source of value in the deal.

passages.title: Emissions Trading Systems
passages.text: An emissions trading system sets a cap on the total amount of greenhouse gases that covered sectors may emit and issues allowances up to that cap. Each allowance permits the emission of one tonne of carbon dioxide or its equivalent. Companies that emit less than their allowances can sell the surplus, while those that emit more must buy additional allowances or face penalties. Because the cap is reduced each year, the supply of allowances shrinks over time, which is intended to push up their price and encourage investment in cleaner technology. In the early years of several systems, too many allowances were issued, often for free, and prices fell to levels too low to change behaviour. Reforms have since removed surplus allowances from the market, and prices in the largest system have risen several-fold over the past decade. Higher prices raise costs for energy-intensive industries such as steel and cement, which argue that they face competition from producers in countries without similar schemes. To address this, some jurisdictions are introducing border adjustments, which charge importers a price on the emissions embedded in certain goods. Trading partners have criticised these measures as a form of protectionism. Supporters reply that without them, production and emissions would simply move abroad, a problem known as carbon leakage.

passages.title: Buybacks Versus Dividends
passages.text: Companies can return cash to shareholders in two main ways: by paying dividends or by buying back their own shares. In a buyback, the company purchases shares on the market and usually cancels them, so each remaining share represents a larger fraction of the business. Because earnings are then divided among fewer shares, earnings per share rises even if total profit is unchanged. In jurisdictions where dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains, buybacks also allow shareholders who do not wish to sell to avoid receiving taxable income. Buybacks have overtaken dividends as the larger form of cash return in some markets. Supporters say buybacks are more flexible than dividends, since investors tend to view a dividend cut as a sign of trouble, whereas a buyback programme can be scaled back quietly. Critics argue that buybacks can be used to meet earnings-per-share targets linked to executive pay, and that cash spent on buybacks might otherwise be invested in research, equipment or wages. Evidence on this second point is mixed: some studies find that companies carrying out large buybacks invest less, while others find that they simply have fewer attractive investment opportunities. A buyback creates value for remaining shareholders only if the shares are bought at less than their intrinsic value; paying too much transfers value to the shareholders who sell.

passages.title: AI Assistants in Customer Support
passages.text: Many companies are deploying software assistants based on large language models to handle customer enquiries. In a study of one company's support centre, agents who were given access to an AI assistant resolved about 14% more enquiries per hour on average than before. The gains were not evenly distributed: the least experienced agents improved by more than a third, while the most experienced saw little or no change. The researchers suggest that the assistant spread the practices of the best agents to newer colleagues, since its suggestions were based on records of past successful conversations. Customer satisfaction scores also rose slightly, and fewer customers asked to speak to a manager. However, the study covered a single company over about a year, and the authors caution against assuming that similar gains will occur elsewhere. Other observers raise longer-term questions. If junior employees rely on the assistant, they may develop expertise more slowly, and if experienced staff see no benefit, they may be less willing to share the knowledge that trains future systems. There is also the question of how gains are shared. Higher productivity could allow a company to handle the same volume of enquiries with fewer staff, to improve service, or to raise wages, and the study does not indicate which of these the company chose.

passages.title: Office Property After the Pandemic
passages.text: Office vacancy rates in many large cities have risen since 2020, as companies have reduced the space they lease in response to hybrid working. The impact has been uneven. Demand for modern, energy-efficient buildings in central locations has remained relatively strong, and rents for such space have in some cases increased, as employers seek to attract staff back to the office. By contrast, older buildings with poor energy ratings have seen vacancy rise most sharply, and some may require expensive renovation to meet tightening environmental standards. Higher interest rates have added to the pressure. Property values are often estimated by dividing a building's annual rental income by a capitalisation rate, or yield, which tends to move with interest rates. A building generating 5 million euros of rent valued at a yield of 4% is worth 125 million euros; if the yield rises to 5%, its value falls to 100 million euros, even if the rent is unchanged. Owners who borrowed heavily against such buildings may find that their loans now exceed the value of the property. Some cities are encouraging the conversion of empty offices into housing, but conversions are often costly because office buildings tend to have deep floor plates that leave many interior areas without natural light.

passages.title: Succession in Family Businesses
passages.text: Family-owned firms account for a large share of companies in many European economies, including a significant number of medium-sized manufacturers. One of the most difficult moments in the life of such a firm is the transfer of control from one generation to the next. Surveys suggest that fewer than half of family business owners have a documented succession plan, even among those expecting to retire within five years. When no family member is willing or able to take over, the main alternatives are to appoint an external manager while the family retains ownership, or to sell the business, either to a strategic buyer or to a private equity fund. Sales to private equity have become more common, partly because funds can offer the founder the option of retaining a minority stake and remaining involved for a transition period. Some founders are reluctant to sell to private equity because they fear that the new owners will prioritise short-term returns over the firm's long-standing relationships with employees and the local community. Research comparing family firms run by descendants of the founder with those run by external managers has produced mixed results, partly because firms that appoint outsiders may differ in other ways, for instance in size or sector. What most advisers agree on is that planning should begin several years before the intended handover.

passages.title: The Venture Capital Cycle
passages.text: Venture capital funds invest in young companies with high growth potential, in exchange for a minority stake. Because most start-ups fail, a fund's returns typically depend on a small number of investments that grow very large, which can compensate for losses on the rest. Funds usually have a life of around ten years: capital is invested in the first few years and returned to investors when portfolio companies are sold or listed on a stock exchange. Activity in the industry is strongly cyclical. In periods of low interest rates, investors seeking higher returns committed record amounts to venture funds, and start-up valuations rose sharply. When rates increased, valuations of listed technology companies fell, and private valuations followed with a delay, since they are only reset when a company raises new money. Some start-ups delayed fundraising to avoid a 'down round', in which new shares are sold at a lower price than in the previous round, diluting existing shareholders and often damaging staff morale. Others accepted terms that protected new investors, such as preferential rights to be repaid first in a sale. The number of companies listing on stock exchanges also fell sharply, which lengthened the time funds needed to return capital. Despite these difficulties, investment in certain areas, notably artificial intelligence, continued to attract substantial funding.

passages.title: Hedging Currency Risk
passages.text: Companies that sell abroad or buy inputs in foreign currencies are exposed to movements in exchange rates. A European manufacturer that invoices a US customer 10 million dollars, payable in three months, will receive fewer euros if the dollar weakens before payment arrives. To reduce this uncertainty, many firms use forward contracts, which fix today the exchange rate at which a future amount will be converted. A forward removes the risk of loss from an adverse movement, but it also removes the gain the firm would have made had the currency moved in its favour. Options offer a different trade-off: the buyer pays an upfront premium for the right, but not the obligation, to exchange at a set rate, and so retains the benefit of favourable movements. Not all exposure is hedged. Many companies hedge a declining share of expected revenues further into the future, for example 80% of the next quarter's foreign sales but only 30% of sales expected in a year's time, because forecasts become less reliable over longer horizons. Some firms also reduce exposure without financial instruments, by matching costs and revenues in the same currency, for instance by locating production in the markets where they sell. Hedging can smooth reported results, but it cannot protect a company indefinitely from a lasting shift in exchange rates.

passages.title: Rethinking Performance Reviews
passages.text: Annual performance reviews have long been a standard feature of corporate life, but a number of large employers have scaled them back or abandoned numerical ratings altogether. Critics argue that a once-a-year conversation is too infrequent to guide behaviour, that ratings encourage employees to focus on their score rather than on development, and that managers spend many hours on a process that staff often regard as unfair. In place of the annual cycle, some firms have introduced frequent informal check-ins between managers and their team members, sometimes as often as every two weeks. Early reports from these companies describe higher employee engagement, although engagement is measured through surveys that were themselves redesigned at the same time. Removing ratings has created new difficulties. Decisions about pay and promotion still have to be made, and without a documented rating, managers may rely more heavily on their impressions, which can be influenced by how visible or self-promoting an employee is. Several firms that dropped ratings later reintroduced a simplified version, typically with three or four categories rather than five or more. Research suggests that the frequency and quality of feedback matter more than the presence or absence of a rating, but quality is difficult to ensure across thousands of managers.

passages.title: Patents and Generic Medicines
passages.text: A new medicine typically takes more than ten years to develop, and most candidate drugs fail during clinical trials. To allow companies to recover these costs, patents grant the inventor exclusive rights for twenty years from the date of filing. Because patents are usually filed early in development, the period of exclusive sales after a drug reaches the market is often considerably shorter, sometimes around ten years. When the patent expires, other manufacturers can produce generic versions, which must be shown to be equivalent to the original but do not need to repeat the full clinical trials. Prices typically fall sharply once several generic producers enter the market, and the original manufacturer may lose most of its sales of the drug within a year or two, a drop known as the 'patent cliff'. Companies respond in several ways. Some seek additional patents on new formulations or manufacturing methods, a practice that critics describe as 'evergreening' when the changes offer little benefit to patients. Others acquire smaller companies with promising drugs in development in order to replace revenue that is about to expire. Biological medicines, which are produced from living cells, face a different situation: their copies, known as biosimilars, are more expensive to develop and approve, so prices tend to fall less steeply after exclusivity ends.

passages.title: Data Centres and the Power Grid
passages.text: The rapid growth of cloud computing and artificial intelligence has made data centres one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in several countries. A large modern facility can draw as much power as a medium-sized town, and the chips used to train AI models consume considerably more energy than conventional servers. In some regions, grid operators have warned that requests to connect new data centres exceed the capacity that can be added in the coming years, and waiting times for a grid connection have stretched to several years. Operators of data centres have responded in several ways. Many have signed long-term contracts to buy electricity from new wind and solar projects, and a few have announced plans to source power from nuclear plants. Others are locating new facilities in regions with spare grid capacity or cooler climates, which reduce the energy needed for cooling. Efficiency has also improved: the ratio of total facility energy to the energy used by the computing equipment itself has fallen at many sites, meaning that less power is spent on cooling and other overheads. Even so, forecasts of future demand vary widely, because they depend on assumptions about how quickly AI will be adopted and how much more efficient future chips will become. Some analysts warn that if adoption is slower than expected, utilities that invest heavily in new capacity may struggle to recover their costs.

passages.title: Pricing an IPO
passages.text: When a company first sells shares to the public in an initial public offering, or IPO, the price is usually set by the company and its banks after a process called bookbuilding, in which institutional investors indicate how many shares they would buy and at what price. On average, shares in IPOs have closed their first day of trading above the offer price, a pattern known as underpricing. Several explanations have been proposed. One is that the banks, which also serve institutional clients, have an incentive to leave some gains for those clients. Another is that investors who know less about the company need a discount to compensate for the risk of buying overpriced shares. A third is that a strong first-day rise generates publicity that benefits the company in later fundraising. Underpricing represents a cost to existing shareholders, who sell shares or are diluted at a lower price than the market is willing to pay. Partly for this reason, some companies have chosen a direct listing, in which existing shares begin trading without a traditional offering and the opening price is determined by orders on the exchange. A direct listing avoids underpricing and reduces fees, but until recent rule changes it did not allow the company to raise new capital, and it is generally considered suitable only for well-known companies that do not need banks to market their shares.

items.stem: Most firms now accept that hybrid working should continue.

steps: Cerca la parte che parla della continuazione del lavoro ibrido: è l'ultima frase.
Il testo dice: «whether hybrid working should continue, which most firms now accept».
L'affermazione riformula fedelmente questa frase, quindi è True.
explanation.shortcut: «Most firms» e «continue» compaiono insieme nell'ultima frase: trovala e confronta parola per parola.
explanation.trap: Farsi influenzare dalle critiche agli anchor days e pensare che si discuta ancora se continuare. Il testo dice che il dibattito si sta spostando dal se al come.
explanation.rule: Se l'affermazione è una parafrasi fedele di una frase del testo, la risposta è True.

items.stem: Research consistently shows that hybrid working raises employee productivity.

steps: Il testo dice esplicitamente: «the evidence on productivity is less clear».
Poi descrive risultati discordanti: «Some studies report that individual output on focused tasks rises», mentre «others find that collaboration and the informal transfer of knowledge suffer».
Se gli studi non concordano, la ricerca non mostra un risultato «consistently». L'affermazione è contraddetta: False.
explanation.shortcut: Avverbi come «consistently», «always», «clearly» sono assoluti: cerca nel testo un segnale di disaccordo o incertezza.
explanation.trap: Ricordare solo la frase sull'aumento di output nei focused tasks e rispondere True, oppure scegliere Cannot say perché le evidenze sono incerte. Ma l'incertezza dichiarata contraddice proprio la parola «consistently».
explanation.rule: Se il testo dice che le prove sono contrastanti, un'affermazione che le presenta come univoche è False.

items.stem: Junior staff are more likely than senior staff to leave an employer that requires full-time office attendance.

steps: Il dato sulla retention viene da un sondaggio: «64% would consider leaving their employer if required to return to the office full time».
Il sondaggio non distingue tra junior e senior.
I junior compaiono solo in un altro punto, a proposito dell'apprendimento: «particularly for junior staff who learn by observing colleagues».
Il testo non confronta i due gruppi sulla propensione a lasciare l'azienda, quindi Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Chiediti: il testo fornisce dati su entrambi i gruppi per la stessa variabile? Se no, è Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Unire la frase sui junior (che parla di apprendimento) con quella sul 64% (che parla di dimissioni) e costruire un confronto che il testo non fa.
explanation.rule: Un confronto tra gruppi è True o False solo se il testo dà informazioni su entrambi i gruppi per lo stesso aspetto.

items.stem: Most of the employees surveyed would leave their employer if they were required to return to the office full time.

steps: Il dato è: «64% would consider leaving their employer if required to return to the office full time».
Il 64% è la maggioranza, ma il testo parla di «would consider leaving», cioè di valutare l'uscita, non di uscire davvero.
Il testo non dice quanti dipendenti se ne andrebbero realmente, quindi Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Confronta il verbo: «consider leaving» non è «leave». Quando l'affermazione rafforza il verbo del testo, di solito la risposta è Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Vedere che 64% è più della metà e rispondere True senza notare che l'affermazione trasforma un'intenzione ipotetica in un'azione certa.
explanation.rule: Intenzioni, opinioni e previsioni riportate nel testo non dimostrano comportamenti effettivi.

items.stem: Under supply chain finance, the bank is repaid by the supplier on the invoice's original due date.

steps: Il testo dice: «the bank is repaid by the buyer on the original due date».
L'affermazione mette il supplier al posto del buyer. Il supplier anzi riceve il pagamento anticipato dalla banca.
Il soggetto è sbagliato, quindi l'affermazione è contraddetta: False.
explanation.shortcut: Nelle domande su chi fa cosa, sottolinea il soggetto nel testo e confrontalo con quello dell'affermazione.
explanation.trap: Leggere di fretta, riconoscere «repaid» e «original due date» e rispondere True senza controllare chi rimborsa.
explanation.rule: Se l'affermazione cambia il soggetto di un'azione descritta nel testo, è False.

items.stem: The cost of early payment for a supplier depends on the buyer's credit rating rather than on its own.

steps: Il costo per il supplier è lo sconto applicato al pagamento anticipato (il pagamento arriva «minus a small discount»).
Il testo dice: «the discount is based on the buyer's credit rating rather than the supplier's».
L'affermazione riformula esattamente questo concetto: True.
explanation.shortcut: Cerca «credit rating»: compare una sola volta e risolve la domanda.
explanation.trap: Ragionare con conoscenza esterna (di solito il costo del credito dipende dal rischio di chi riceve i soldi) e rispondere False.
explanation.rule: Rispondi solo in base al testo, anche quando contraddice la tua intuizione su come funziona di solito il mercato.

items.stem: Under recent disclosure standards, companies must reclassify supply chain finance balances as debt.

steps: L'ultima frase dice che i nuovi standard richiedono di riportare «the terms and size of such programmes».
Subito dopo aggiunge: «although they do not oblige companies to reclassify the amounts as debt».
L'affermazione dice l'opposto della seconda parte della frase: False.
explanation.shortcut: Le frasi con «although» o «however» contengono spesso il dettaglio decisivo: leggi sempre fino in fondo.
explanation.trap: Fermarsi a «require companies to report» e confondere l'obbligo di disclosure con l'obbligo di riclassificare come debito.
explanation.rule: Distingui l'obbligo di informare dall'obbligo di cambiare il trattamento contabile.

items.stem: Buyers use supply chain finance mainly in order to extend their payment terms.

steps: Il testo dice che per i buyer l'accordo «makes it possible to extend payment terms without damaging relationships with suppliers».
Dire che una cosa è possibile non significa che sia il motivo principale per cui viene usata.
Il testo non indica quali siano le motivazioni prevalenti dei buyer, quindi Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: «Makes it possible» descrive una possibilità, «mainly» descrive una priorità: sono informazioni diverse.
explanation.trap: Rispondere True perché l'affermazione è coerente con il testo e plausibile nella realtà, anche se il testo non parla di motivazione principale.
explanation.rule: Possibilità non equivale a prevalenza: per «mainly» o «most» serve un'indicazione esplicita.

items.stem: Hydrometallurgical processes recover a higher share of lithium than pyrometallurgical processes.

steps: Sui processi pirometallurgici il testo dice che «recover lithium poorly».
Sui processi idrometallurgici dice che «recover a higher share of lithium, cobalt and nickel».
Il confronto sul litio è esplicito e coincide con l'affermazione: True.
explanation.shortcut: Individua le due frasi parallele (una per metodo) e confronta solo la parola «lithium».
explanation.trap: Farsi frenare dallo svantaggio degli idrometallurgici (devono essere «carefully sorted and pre-treated»). Lo svantaggio riguarda un altro aspetto e non cambia il confronto sul litio.
explanation.rule: Un confronto è True se il testo descrive entrambi i termini in modo coerente con l'affermazione.

items.stem: By the time a battery is no longer suitable for driving, it has lost most of its original capacity.

steps: Il testo dice che la batteria «retains around 70 to 80% of its original capacity» quando non è più adatta alla guida.
Se ne conserva il 70-80%, ne ha perso il 20-30%, cioè molto meno della metà.
Aver perso «most» della capacità è contraddetto dal dato: False.
explanation.shortcut: Quando il testo indica ciò che resta e l'affermazione ciò che si perde, calcola subito il complemento (100% meno il dato).
explanation.trap: Pensare per intuizione che una batteria non più adatta alla guida debba essere quasi esaurita, invece di usare il numero del testo.
explanation.rule: Se testo e affermazione usano grandezze complementari (trattenuto contro perso), fai il calcolo prima di rispondere.

items.stem: Falling cobalt prices prompted manufacturers to design batteries that use less cobalt.

steps: Il testo collega i design a basso cobalto a «concerns about the ethical sourcing of cobalt».
Il calo dei prezzi del cobalto è citato solo come causa dei margini compressi dei recycler: «several recyclers found their margins squeezed».
«Meanwhile» indica solo contemporaneità, non un legame causale tra prezzi e scelte dei produttori.
Il testo non dice che il calo dei prezzi abbia spinto i produttori, ma nemmeno lo esclude: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Individua la causa che il testo assegna a ciascun effetto. Una causa diversa, non citata ma non esclusa, porta a Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Rispondere False perché il testo indica un'altra causa. Il testo non dice che quella etica sia l'unica ragione, quindi non contraddice l'affermazione.
explanation.rule: Due fatti contemporanei non sono collegati da causa ed effetto a meno che il testo lo dica.

items.stem: Industry groups are opposed to minimum recycled-content requirements for new batteries.

steps: Il testo dice: «Industry groups broadly support these targets».
La loro critica riguarda solo i tempi: «the deadlines are too ambitious».
Sostenere i target criticandone le scadenze non equivale a opporsi: l'affermazione è contraddetta, False.
explanation.shortcut: Separa l'opinione sull'obiettivo («support these targets») da quella sulle modalità («deadlines»).
explanation.trap: Leggere la critica sulle scadenze come opposizione all'intera misura e rispondere True.
explanation.rule: Una critica ai tempi o ai dettagli di una misura non equivale a opposizione alla misura.

items.stem: Covenant-lite loans do not contain maintenance covenants.

steps: Il testo definisce i covenant-lite: «meaning that they lack maintenance covenants».
«Lack» significa che non li contengono: l'affermazione coincide con la definizione, True.
explanation.shortcut: Le domande su una definizione si risolvono trovando la frase con «meaning that» o «refers to».
explanation.trap: Invertire i due tipi di covenant: chi associa ai bond i maintenance covenants (invece degli incurrence) e ricorda che i covenant-lite «resemble bonds» può rispondere False.
explanation.rule: Le definizioni date nel testo valgono come fatti: usale alla lettera.

items.stem: High-yield bonds have typically been issued without maintenance covenants.

steps: Il testo dice: «high-yield bonds have usually relied on incurrence covenants alone».
«Alone» significa che, di solito, non hanno altri tipi di covenant, quindi niente maintenance covenants.
Conferma: i covenant-lite «resemble bonds in this respect», proprio perché mancano di maintenance covenants. True.
explanation.shortcut: «Alone» e «only» escludono tutto il resto: trasformali in una negazione per verificare l'affermazione.
explanation.trap: Non accorgersi che l'affermazione è formulata in negativo mentre il testo è in positivo, e rispondere Cannot say.
explanation.rule: Una frase con «alone» o «only» implica logicamente l'assenza delle alternative.

items.stem: Covenant-lite structures lead to lower recoveries for lenders when borrowers default.

steps: Il legame tra assenza di covenant e recuperi più bassi è l'opinione dei critici: «Critics respond that... which tends to reduce the amount they recover».
I sostenitori hanno una posizione diversa.
Il testo conclude: «Data from the most recent downturn are not yet sufficient to determine which view is correct».
Se il testo stesso dice che la questione non è risolta, la risposta è Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Quando un'affermazione riporta come fatto la tesi di una parte («critics argue»), controlla se il testo la conferma. Qui dice esplicitamente di no.
explanation.trap: Prendere la tesi dei critici come un fatto e rispondere True, oppure rispondere False confondendo «non dimostrato» con «smentito».
explanation.rule: Un'opinione attribuita a qualcuno non è un fatto: se il testo non la verifica, la risposta è Cannot say.

items.stem: Covenant-lite terms were accepted by lenders at a time when there was strong demand for higher-yielding assets.

steps: Il testo dice: «Lenders accepted these terms during a period of strong demand for higher-yielding assets».
«These terms» si riferisce ai covenant-lite descritti nella frase precedente.
L'affermazione è la stessa frase in forma passiva: True.
explanation.shortcut: Le riformulazioni attivo/passivo non cambiano il significato: riconosci la frase e rispondi.
explanation.trap: Cercare un nesso causale che l'affermazione non richiede. Qui si parla solo di contemporaneità («at a time when»), che il testo conferma.
explanation.rule: Un'affermazione che dice solo «quando» (non «perché») richiede solo la conferma temporale.

items.stem: Over several years, a subscription always costs the customer less than a perpetual licence.

steps: Il testo dice che il costo iniziale è più basso, ma aggiunge: «the total paid over several years can exceed the price of a perpetual licence».
Se il totale può superare il prezzo della licenza, non è vero che costi sempre meno.
L'affermazione assoluta è contraddetta: False.
explanation.shortcut: «Always» nell'affermazione e «can exceed» nel testo: basta un caso possibile contrario per rispondere False.
explanation.trap: Fermarsi a «the upfront cost is lower» e applicarlo all'intero periodo.
explanation.rule: Se il testo ammette anche solo la possibilità del contrario, un'affermazione con «always» è False.

items.stem: Usage-based pricing can make a vendor's revenue vulnerable to a slowdown in its customers' businesses.

steps: Con il usage-based pricing il prezzo dipende dal volume di dati o di transazioni.
Il testo dice che rende i ricavi più difficili da prevedere «since usage can fall sharply when a customer's own business slows».
Se l'utilizzo cala con il rallentamento del cliente, cala anche il ricavo del vendor: True.
explanation.shortcut: Segui la catena: business del cliente rallenta, utilizzo cala, ricavo del vendor cala. Ogni anello è nel testo.
explanation.trap: Rispondere Cannot say perché il testo non usa la parola «vulnerable». Conta il significato, non le parole identiche.
explanation.rule: Un'inferenza diretta, in cui ogni passaggio è scritto nel testo, è True.

items.stem: A company can report net revenue retention above 100% even if some of its existing customers cancelled during the year.

steps: Il testo spiega che un valore sopra il 100% «indicates that expansion within existing accounts more than offsets the revenue lost from customers who cancel or downgrade».
La definizione stessa prevede che ci siano clienti che cancellano: l'espansione degli altri compensa e supera quella perdita.
Quindi le cancellazioni sono compatibili con un valore sopra il 100%: True.
explanation.shortcut: La frase usa «more than offsets»: se qualcosa viene compensato, vuol dire che esiste. Le cancellazioni sono già incluse nella definizione.
explanation.trap: Pensare che sopra il 100% significhi nessuna perdita di clienti e rispondere False.
explanation.rule: Quando una metrica è definita come saldo netto, un valore positivo non esclude componenti negative.

items.stem: Most subscription software vendors offer three pricing tiers.

steps: Il testo dice: «A common approach offers three tiers».
«Common» significa diffuso, ma non indica se riguardi più della metà dei vendor.
Il testo non fornisce la quota di vendor con tre livelli, quindi Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Traduci le parole di quantità: «common», «many», «several» non equivalgono a «most».
explanation.trap: Considerare «common» sinonimo di «most» e rispondere True.
explanation.rule: «Many» o «common» nel testo non bastano a confermare «most»: serve un dato esplicito.

items.stem: Central bank governors are usually appointed by governments.

steps: Il testo dice: «Governments typically appoint central bank governors».
«Typically» equivale a «usually»: l'affermazione è la stessa frase in forma passiva, quindi True.
explanation.shortcut: Cerca «appoint»: compare una sola volta e risolve la domanda.
explanation.trap: Pensare che l'indipendenza della banca centrale escluda qualsiasi ruolo del governo e rispondere False. Il testo dice proprio che «Independence is never absolute».
explanation.rule: Il testo prevale sull'idea che ti sei fatto del concetto: verifica sempre la frase specifica.

items.stem: Central bank independence is the main reason why some countries have experienced lower inflation than others.

steps: Il testo riporta una correlazione: i paesi con banche centrali più indipendenti hanno avuto «on average, experienced lower inflation».
Subito dopo precisa che «economists disagree about how much of this difference is caused by independence itself rather than by other features of those countries».
Se non è chiaro quanta parte della differenza dipenda dall'indipendenza, non si può dire che sia la ragione principale. Il testo non la esclude nemmeno: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Correlazione nel testo più disaccordo sulla causa significa Cannot say per qualsiasi affermazione causale forte («main reason», «caused»).
explanation.trap: Rispondere True perché la correlazione è chiara, oppure False perché esistono altre spiegazioni. Il testo lascia aperta la questione.
explanation.rule: Una correlazione dichiarata non dimostra la causa: se il testo segnala dubbi sul nesso causale, è Cannot say.

items.stem: An independent central bank is entirely free from the influence of the government.

steps: Il testo dice esplicitamente: «Independence is never absolute».
Poi elenca le leve del governo: nomina i governatori, «set their mandates in law and can, in principle, change those laws».
«Entirely free» è quindi contraddetto: False.
explanation.shortcut: «Entirely», «completely», «never» sono parole assolute: qui il testo contiene la negazione esplicita dell'assoluto.
explanation.trap: Basarsi sulla prima frase («operates independently of the government») e ignorare la precisazione successiva.
explanation.rule: Quando il testo qualifica un concetto («never absolute»), un'affermazione che lo rende assoluto è False.

items.stem: Purchases of government bonds since 2008 have exposed central banks to greater political pressure.

steps: Il testo attribuisce questa tesi solo a una parte: «Some commentators argue that this has exposed central banks to greater political pressure».
Altri sostengono il contrario: gli acquisti «do not compromise independence as long as they are reversed in time».
Il testo riporta due opinioni senza stabilire quale sia corretta: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: «Some argue... while others maintain» segnala un dibattito: un'affermazione che sposa una delle due tesi è quasi sempre Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Considerare la frase dei commentatori come un fatto perché è scritta per prima o perché suona plausibile.
explanation.rule: Un'opinione riportata non è un fatto: se il testo non prende posizione, la risposta è Cannot say.

items.stem: Most large graduate employers use online assessments before the interview stage.

steps: Il testo dice che i grandi employer: «most now use online assessments as an early screening stage, before any interview takes place».
L'affermazione riformula la frase mantenendo lo stesso quantificatore («most»): True.
explanation.shortcut: Controlla che il quantificatore sia lo stesso: «most» nel testo e «most» nell'affermazione.
explanation.trap: Pensare che, siccome alcune aziende hanno eliminato i reasoning test, la maggioranza non usi assessment online. Quelle aziende sono «A small number of firms».
explanation.rule: Se soggetto, quantificatore e azione coincidono con il testo, la risposta è True.

items.stem: Unstructured interviews predict later job performance better than well-designed reasoning tests.

steps: Il testo dice che i punteggi dei reasoning test ben progettati «have been shown to predict later job performance better than unstructured interviews do».
L'affermazione inverte i due termini del confronto.
Il confronto è rovesciato rispetto al testo: False.
explanation.shortcut: Nei confronti, identifica chi sta a sinistra e chi a destra di «better than» in entrambe le frasi.
explanation.trap: Riconoscere tutte le parole del testo e rispondere True senza accorgersi dell'inversione.
explanation.rule: Un confronto con i termini invertiti rispetto al testo è False.

items.stem: A candidate's familiarity with the test format can influence the score they achieve.

steps: Il testo dice: «practice is known to improve scores».
Lo collega esplicitamente alla familiarità: la questione è se i test «measure ability or familiarity».
Per questo alcune aziende pubblicano materiali gratuiti «so that all applicants can become familiar with the format». La familiarità incide sul punteggio: True.
explanation.shortcut: Se il testo dice che la pratica migliora i punteggi, ogni affermazione che dice che la familiarità «can influence» il punteggio è True.
explanation.trap: Rispondere Cannot say perché il testo presenta il tema come una critica. Ma «is known to improve scores» è un fatto, non un'opinione.
explanation.rule: Distingui la parte fattuale di una critica («is known to») dalla parte opinabile («raises questions»).

items.stem: Firms that replaced reasoning tests with work-sample tasks have made better hires as a result.

steps: Il testo dice che alcune aziende hanno sostituito i test con «short work-sample tasks».
Poi aggiunge: «there is not yet enough evidence to say whether this produces better hires».
Il testo dichiara che l'informazione non è disponibile: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Frasi come «not yet enough evidence» o «it is unclear» portano direttamente a Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Scegliere False confondendo «non c'è prova che funzioni» con «è provato che non funziona».
explanation.rule: Assenza di prove non è prova del contrario: se il testo dice che non si sa, è Cannot say.

items.stem: Fabless firms manufacture some of their own chips.

steps: Il testo definisce le fabless: «focus entirely on design and outsource all manufacturing».
Se esternalizzano tutta la produzione, non producono nessun chip internamente.
L'affermazione è contraddetta dalla definizione: False.
explanation.shortcut: «All manufacturing» esternalizzato esclude qualsiasi produzione interna, anche parziale.
explanation.trap: Confondere le fabless con gli integrated manufacturers che, alla fine del testo, offrono anche servizi di foundry.
explanation.rule: Se il testo dice «all» o «entirely», qualsiasi «some» di segno opposto è False.

items.stem: Because of high fixed costs, it is important for foundries to run their plants close to full capacity.

steps: Il testo: una foundry può tenere gli impianti «running near full capacity, which is essential given the high fixed costs».
«Essential» è più forte di «important», quindi l'affermazione è coperta.
Anche il nesso causale (i costi fissi elevati) è esplicito: True.
explanation.shortcut: Se il testo usa un termine più forte («essential») di quello dell'affermazione («important»), l'affermazione è confermata.
explanation.trap: Esitare perché le parole non sono identiche. Un'affermazione più debole del testo è sempre coperta.
explanation.rule: Il testo forte conferma l'affermazione debole, mai il contrario.

items.stem: During the recent shortage, foundries gave priority to carmakers because of the size of their orders.

steps: Il testo dice che i carmakers «struggled to obtain the components they needed».
Il motivo: le foundries «prioritised customers with larger and more profitable orders».
Se i carmakers hanno faticato a ottenere i chip proprio per questa regola di priorità, non erano loro i clienti prioritari: False.
explanation.shortcut: Chiediti chi ha beneficiato della priorità: i clienti con ordini più grandi. I carmakers sono citati come quelli in difficoltà.
explanation.trap: Associare «priority» e «larger and more profitable orders» ai carmakers solo perché compaiono nella stessa frase.
explanation.rule: Verifica sempre a quale soggetto il testo collega ciascuna azione.

items.stem: Most leading-edge chip production now takes place at foundries rather than at integrated manufacturers.

steps: Il testo dice solo che «a growing share of production has moved to foundries».
Una quota in crescita non indica se abbia superato la metà.
Il testo cita anche la concentrazione della produzione avanzata «in a small number of locations», ma non dice in quale tipo di azienda.
Senza un dato sulla quota, l'affermazione non è verificabile: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: «Growing share» descrive una direzione, non un livello: non basta per «most».
explanation.trap: Usare conoscenze esterne sul settore dei semiconduttori, che potrebbero far sembrare l'affermazione vera. Nel test conta solo il testo.
explanation.rule: Una tendenza («growing», «rising») non dice nulla sul livello raggiunto: per «most» serve un dato.

items.stem: In an earn-out, part of the purchase price depends on how the business performs after the deal is completed.

steps: Il testo: «part of the purchase price is paid upfront, and further payments are made only if the business meets agreed targets after completion».
Quindi una parte del prezzo è condizionata ai risultati post closing: True.
explanation.shortcut: Le domande di definizione si risolvono con la frase che descrive il meccanismo («Under this arrangement...»).
explanation.trap: Rispondere Cannot say perché l'affermazione non cita i target né il periodo di uno-tre anni. Basta che il meccanismo (una parte del prezzo legata ai risultati dopo il closing) coincida con il testo.
explanation.rule: Se l'affermazione riproduce il meccanismo descritto nel testo, è True.

items.stem: Buyers often deliberately suppress the performance of acquired businesses in order to avoid earn-out payments.

steps: Il testo dice: «Sellers may suspect that the buyer is deliberately suppressing performance to avoid paying».
È un sospetto attribuito ai venditori, introdotto da «may suspect», non un fatto accertato.
Il testo non dice quanto spesso accada, né se accada davvero: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Verbi come «suspect», «believe», «claim» indicano il punto di vista di qualcuno: non trasformarli in fatti.
explanation.trap: Collegare il sospetto alle dispute frequenti («frequently lead to disputes») e concludere che il comportamento sia frequente. Le dispute possono nascere anche solo dal sospetto.
explanation.rule: Un sospetto o un'accusa riportati nel testo non provano il comportamento: Cannot say.

items.stem: Earn-out targets are always based on financial measures such as revenue or EBITDA.

steps: Il testo: i target sono «most often based on revenue or EBITDA».
Poi: «some deals use non-financial milestones, such as obtaining regulatory approval».
Esistono target non finanziari, quindi «always» è contraddetto: False.
explanation.shortcut: «Most often» nel testo segnala già che ci sono eccezioni: cerca l'eccezione e hai la risposta.
explanation.trap: Fermarsi alla prima metà della frase e rispondere True.
explanation.rule: Un'affermazione con «always» è False se il testo cita anche una sola eccezione.

items.stem: After completion, decisions taken by the buyer can affect how much the seller ultimately receives under an earn-out.

steps: Il testo: «the buyer controls decisions on pricing, investment and the allocation of shared costs, all of which can affect whether targets are reached».
I pagamenti dell'earn-out avvengono «only if the business meets agreed targets».
Se le decisioni del buyer incidono sul raggiungimento dei target, incidono sull'importo pagato al seller: True.
explanation.shortcut: Collega due anelli scritti nel testo: decisioni del buyer, raggiungimento dei target, pagamento.
explanation.trap: Rispondere Cannot say perché il testo non dice in una sola frase «the buyer affects the payment». Un'inferenza a due passaggi entrambi espliciti è valida.
explanation.rule: Se A influenza B e B determina C, entrambi scritti nel testo, l'affermazione che A può influenzare C è True.

items.stem: In the trial described, a majority of firms continued with the four-day week after the trial ended.

steps: Il testo: «a majority chose to continue with the arrangement after the trial ended».
«The arrangement» è la settimana di quattro giorni: l'affermazione coincide, True.
explanation.shortcut: Cerca la parola «majority» e verifica il soggetto: sono le aziende partecipanti al trial.
explanation.trap: Lasciarsi influenzare dalle obiezioni degli scettici, che riguardano la generalizzabilità dei risultati, non il dato in sé.
explanation.rule: Le critiche al metodo non cambiano i fatti riportati sul campione.

items.stem: Working a four-day week caused the reduction in employees' sick days during the trial.

steps: Il testo dice solo che i dipendenti hanno riportato «lower levels of stress and fewer sick days».
Non afferma che la riduzione sia causata dalla settimana corta: riporta due fatti nello stesso periodo.
Gli scettici segnalano anzi che le aziende «volunteered» ed erano probabilmente le più adatte, quindi altri fattori possono avere contribuito.
Il nesso causale non è né confermato né escluso: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Un trial senza gruppo di controllo, con partecipanti volontari, non permette di affermare la causa. Cerca «caused»: se il testo non lo dice, è Cannot say.
explanation.trap: Considerare la causa ovvia perché il risultato è avvenuto durante il trial.
explanation.rule: Ciò che accade durante un esperimento non è automaticamente causato dall'esperimento, a meno che il testo lo dica.

items.stem: Under a compressed schedule, employees work fewer total hours than under a standard five-day week.

steps: Il testo definisce i compressed schedules: «employees work the same total hours over four longer days».
Stesse ore totali, non meno ore: False.
È la differenza chiave con la settimana di 32 ore, in cui le ore si riducono davvero.
explanation.shortcut: Distingui i due modelli del testo: four-day week (meno ore) e compressed schedule (stesse ore, giornate più lunghe).
explanation.trap: Confondere il compressed schedule con la settimana di quattro giorni da circa 32 ore descritta all'inizio.
explanation.rule: Quando il testo descrive due modelli simili, verifica a quale si riferisce l'affermazione.

items.stem: The results of the trial may not apply equally to every type of organisation.

steps: Il testo indica che i settori con copertura continua, come «healthcare and retail, face a different challenge», perché ridurre le ore implica assumere o riorganizzare i turni.
Questa frase è nella voce dell'autore, non solo degli scettici.
Se alcuni settori affrontano problemi diversi, i risultati non sono ugualmente applicabili a tutti: l'affermazione, formulata con «may», è True.
explanation.shortcut: Un'affermazione prudente («may not») è True se il testo fornisce anche un solo motivo concreto per cui potrebbe accadere.
explanation.trap: Rispondere Cannot say pensando che il limite sia solo l'opinione degli scettici. La frase sui settori a copertura continua è un fatto riportato dall'autore.
explanation.rule: Le affermazioni formulate con «may» o «can» richiedono solo che il testo ne mostri la possibilità.

items.stem: The same company can receive very different ESG ratings from different providers.

steps: Il testo dice: «A company can be rated a leader by one provider and a laggard by another».
Leader e laggard sono valutazioni opposte, quindi molto diverse: True.
explanation.shortcut: Cerca l'esempio concreto nel testo: «leader» contro «laggard» risolve subito la domanda.
explanation.trap: Pensare che i rating debbano convergere come quelli creditizi. Il testo dice l'opposto: la correlazione tra provider è «much lower».
explanation.rule: Se il testo fornisce un esempio che coincide con l'affermazione, la risposta è True.

items.stem: Like credit ratings, ESG ratings are designed to estimate a single, well-defined outcome.

steps: Il testo apre il confronto con «Unlike credit ratings, which estimate a single, well-defined outcome».
Gli ESG ratings invece «combine dozens of indicators».
L'affermazione dice «Like» dove il testo dice «Unlike»: False.
explanation.shortcut: Guarda la prima parola del confronto: «Unlike» contro «Like» è una contraddizione diretta.
explanation.trap: Riconoscere l'espressione «single, well-defined outcome» e rispondere True senza notare che il testo la riferisce solo ai credit ratings.
explanation.rule: Se l'affermazione attribuisce a un soggetto una caratteristica che il testo riserva a un altro per contrasto, è False.

items.stem: Larger companies tend to receive higher ESG scores because they perform better on environmental and social issues.

steps: Il testo conferma che le aziende più grandi «tend to receive higher scores».
La spiegazione che dà il testo è diversa: hanno «more resources to devote to reporting» e i dati vengono in gran parte dalle loro disclosure.
L'idea che il punteggio premi la disclosure e non la performance è dei critici («Critics argue»), quindi non esclude che le grandi aziende performino anche meglio.
Il testo non conferma né smentisce la causa indicata nell'affermazione: Cannot say.
explanation.shortcut: Separa il fatto (punteggi più alti) dalla causa (performance). Il fatto è nel testo, la causa proposta no, e non è esclusa.
explanation.trap: Rispondere False perché il testo offre un'altra spiegazione. Una spiegazione alternativa non esclude quella dell'affermazione, a meno che il testo lo dica.
explanation.rule: Una causa diversa da quella indicata nel testo, ma non esclusa, porta a Cannot say.

items.stem: New regulations require all ESG rating providers to use the same methodology.

steps: Le nuove regole chiedono di «explain their methodologies» e gestire i conflitti di interesse.
Il testo aggiunge: «These rules do not, however, prescribe a single methodology».
L'affermazione dice esattamente il contrario: False.
explanation.shortcut: Le frasi con «however» spesso contengono il limite decisivo di una misura: leggile sempre.
explanation.trap: Confondere l'obbligo di spiegare la metodologia con l'obbligo di adottarne una comune.
explanation.rule: Obbligo di trasparenza non equivale a obbligo di uniformità.

items.stem: Just-in-time production reduces the amount of cash tied up in working capital.

steps: Il just-in-time punta a minimizzare le scorte.
Il testo dice: «Holding less stock reduces the cash tied up in working capital».
L'affermazione coincide: True.
explanation.shortcut: Collega just-in-time a «less stock» (prima frase) e poi trova l'effetto sulla cassa nella seconda.
explanation.trap: Lasciarsi distrarre dalla debolezza del modello (la vulnerabilità alle interruzioni), che non c'entra con il capitale circolante.
explanation.rule: Un vantaggio elencato nel testo resta vero anche se il testo cita poi degli svantaggi.

items.stem: Under just-in-time production, defective parts are likely to be detected sooner.

steps: Il testo dice che avere meno scorte «exposes quality problems quickly, since there is no buffer to hide defective parts».
Senza un buffer che nasconda i pezzi difettosi, questi emergono prima: l'affermazione è una parafrasi, True.
explanation.shortcut: «Exposes quality problems quickly» equivale a «detected sooner»: riconosci il sinonimo.
explanation.trap: Cercare le stesse parole («detected», «sooner») e rispondere Cannot say quando non le trovi.
explanation.rule: Nel verbal conta il significato: una parafrasi fedele è True.

items.stem: The passage's estimate of roughly 40 million euros of additional working capital already includes the cost of storing the extra inventory.

steps: Verifica il numero: 1 miliardo / 365 giorni = circa 2,74 milioni di vendite al giorno; 15 giorni in più (da 30 a 45) x 2,74 milioni = circa 41 milioni, cioè «roughly an additional 40 million euros».
Il testo però delimita il perimetro della stima: è capitale circolante immobilizzato «before considering the cost of storage and the risk that goods become obsolete».
«Before considering» significa che i costi di magazzino sono esclusi e andrebbero aggiunti ai 40 milioni. L'affermazione dice che sono già inclusi: False.
explanation.shortcut: Quando un numero nel testo è accompagnato da «before» o «excluding», verifica se l'affermazione lo usa con il perimetro corretto.
explanation.trap: Verificare solo che il calcolo dei 40 milioni torni e rispondere True, senza leggere il perimetro del dato.
